source: Motion Under a Time-Varying Force
Integrate F(t)/m to find the velocity when the force changes with time.
Students use the final force as if it had acted the whole time.

Newton's Second Law Along an Axis used forces that stay the same. Real pushes rarely do: a motor ramps up, a gust fades, a bat touches a ball for a few milliseconds. Newton's second law still holds at every instant, so the acceleration simply follows the force, and Velocity and Position from Acceleration does the rest.

With a net force $F(t)$ on a mass $m$: $$a(t) = \dfrac{F(t)}{m}, \qquad v(t) = v_0 + \dfrac{1}{m}\int_0^t F(t')\,dt'.$$ The change in velocity is the area under the force–time graph divided by the mass.

$F = ma$ is a statement about one instant: the net force now sets the acceleration now. Over a tiny time $dt$ the velocity changes by $dv = a\,dt = \dfrac{F}{m}\,dt$. Adding up all those small changes is an integral. The quantity $\int F\,dt$ is the impulse, which you'll meet again in Impulse as an Integral.
$F(t) = 6t$ on a 3 kg cart. The area from 0 to 4 s is $48\ \text{N·s}$, so the cart gains $48/3 = 16\ \text{m/s}$.
A $3\ \text{kg}$ cart starts from rest on a frictionless track, pushed by $F(t) = 6t$ (N, s). Find its speed and position at $t = 4\ \text{s}$.
A force that grows
$v = 16\ \text{m/s}$, $x \approx 21.3\ \text{m}$.
$a(t) = F/m = 2t\ \text{m/s}^2$.
$x(t) = \int_0^t t'^2\,dt' = \tfrac{1}{3}t^3$, so $x(4) = \tfrac{64}{3} \approx 21.3\ \text{m}$.
A $5\ \text{kg}$ block on ice starts from rest. A push $F(t) = 40 - 10t$ (N, s) acts until it reaches zero. How fast is the block moving then?
A push that fades out
The force reaches zero at $t = 4\ \text{s}$.
$$\Delta v = \dfrac{1}{5}\int_0^4 (40 - 10t)\,dt = \dfrac{1}{5}\left[40t - 5t^2\right]_0^4 = \dfrac{80}{5} = 16\ \text{m/s}$$
Geometrically, the area is a triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2}(4)(40) = 80\ \text{N·s}$.

Using the final force as if it had acted the whole time. For the first cart, the force at 4 s is 24 N; $24 \times 4/3 = 32\ \text{m/s}$, twice the true 16 m/s, because the push was weaker early on. Using the starting force goes wrong the other way. Check: the answer must equal the area under the actual $F$–$t$ graph divided by $m$. A rectangle drawn at the final height is far bigger than the triangle under $F = 6t$.

If several forces act, add them first: $F_{\text{net}}(t) = F_{\text{push}}(t) - f_k$, and integrate the net force. The integral of one force alone gives only that force's share of the change in momentum.
